name: Gastric sleeve

lead: Sleeve gastrectomy removes most of the stomach, leaving a narrow tube. It is a medical treatment for severe obesity and, according to Wikipedia, the most commonly performed bariatric operation worldwide. The appearance payoff people link to it is large fat loss, giving a leaner body and slimmer face.

Removing roughly three quarters or more of the stomach limits how much food can be eaten and removes the part that produces the appetite hormone ghrelin. Research also describes effects on gut hormones and glucose handling beyond weight loss alone. Systematic reviews report weight loss and resolution of conditions like type 2 diabetes comparable to gastric bypass. It is studied as a medical treatment, not a cosmetic one, and no studies on appearance outcomes were identified.

paras: It is usually done laparoscopically under general anaesthesia, with eligibility set by clinical guidelines based on body mass index and health conditions. Afterwards people follow staged diets and vitamin supplementation, and weight loss builds over many months.

Documented risks include staple-line leaks, bleeding, clots, infection, reflux, nausea and vomiting, vitamin and thiamine deficiencies (including rare Wernicke encephalopathy), gastric dilation, and weight regain that may lead to revision surgery. The operation is considered irreversible.

web.title: Effects of Bariatric Surgery on Facial Features

angle.text: A reduced stomach leads to large, sustained weight loss, which users link to a leaner body and slimmer face. It is studied for weight loss and diabetes in severe obesity, with documented surgical and nutritional risks.

lead: Sleeve gastrectomy, usually called the gastric sleeve, is a bariatric operation, usually laparoscopic, in which roughly 75 to 85 percent of the stomach is removed along its greater curvature, leaving a narrow, banana-sized tube [1]. It is a medical treatment for severe obesity and obesity-related conditions such as type 2 diabetes [2][3], and it has been the most commonly performed bariatric operation worldwide since about 2013 [1][4].

Its link to appearance runs through weight loss. A smaller stomach and removal of the ghrelin-producing part of it reduce appetite and intake, patients commonly lose 50 to 70 percent of their excess weight over two years [1], and a leaner body and face can follow. In ascension and body-transformation circles it is sometimes discussed as the most dramatic route to a slimmer frame. Clinicians stress that it is prescribed for health reasons, not as a cosmetic operation, and that it is irreversible and carries surgical and nutritional risks [1][4].

The operation grew out of the duodenal switch. Surgeons in the 1980s and 1990s found that the sleeve portion alone produced substantial weight loss in very heavy patients, and by the 2000s it was studied as a stand-alone operation [1][5]. Randomised trials such as SLEEVEPASS have followed patients for ten years and compared it with gastric bypass [6]. Eligibility was widened in 2022 when the ASMBS and IFSO replaced the 1991 NIH criteria [7], and more recent coverage compares surgical results with injectable GLP-1 drugs [8].

paras: The surgeon makes a longitudinal resection of the stomach starting from the antrum about 5 to 6 cm from the pylorus and finishing near the cardia. The remaining stomach is calibrated over a tube called a bougie, usually 36 to 40 Fr, and the remaining stomach is roughly 150 mL.[1] A first-in-human trial tested a fluorescence-guided calibration tube during sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass, with 21 sleeve and 10 bypass procedures.[9] Variants include banded sleeve gastrectomy, which places a band to limit dilation of the sleeve.[10]

Weight loss comes from smaller stomach volume and from removal of the portion that produces ghrelin, the hormone that stimulates appetite.[1] Wikipedia also notes improvements in glucose handling before major weight loss has occurred, which it relates to reduced gastric volume, changes in gut peptides and expression of genes involved in glucose absorption.[1]

The operation began as the restrictive part of the duodenal switch and later as the first stage of a two-step operation in extremely obese patients for whom gastric bypass was judged too risky; the weight loss after the first stage was good enough that it began to be studied alone [1]. Bariatric Times traces the lineage in more detail: Lawrence Tretbar reported weight loss after a tubular stomach in 1976, and Doug Hess of Bowling Green, Ohio performed the first open sleeve as part of a duodenal switch in March 1988 [5].

Between 1997 and 2001 Gary Anthone limited a duodenal switch to a sleeve in a 13-year-old and then performed 21 open sleeves in high-risk super-obese patients, with roughly 40 to 50 percent excess-weight loss [5]. In 1999 Gagner and colleagues showed a laparoscopic duodenal switch was feasible in a pig model, and between 2001 and 2003 Gagner staged the bypass by performing a laparoscopic sleeve first; seven patients with BMIs of 58 to 71 averaged 33 percent excess-weight loss after the first stage [5]. The San Francisco group of Johnston and colleagues, who performed the Magenstrasse and Mill operation, reported about 60 percent excess-weight loss at five years in 100 patients and went on to offer a tighter sleeve to lower-BMI patients, reporting 75 to 85 percent at two years in their first 216 patients in 2007 [5].

A 2003 report described reoperative sleeve gastrectomy after failed duodenal switch [11], a 2006 study asked whether gastric dilation limits the sleeve as a sole operation [12], and a 2008 paper reviewed indications for it as a primary procedure [2]. The Second International Consensus Summit for Sleeve Gastrectomy met in Miami in March 2009 and heard five-year excess-weight-loss figures of 42 to 80 percent in a limited number of patients [5]. A combined liver transplantation and sleeve protocol was reported in 2013 [13]. In October 2022 the IFSO and ASMBS published joint guidelines replacing the 1991 NIH statement [7].

The 1991 NIH consensus limited surgery to a BMI of 40 or higher, or 35 or higher with an obesity-related condition [4]. The 2022 ASMBS/IFSO guidelines recommend surgery for adults with a BMI above 35 regardless of other conditions, and say it may be recommended at BMI above 30 for people with diabetes or those unable to sustain long-term weight loss [7]. They suggest lower thresholds for Asian populations, with surgery offered at BMI 27.5 or higher [7][4]. The guidelines also open eligibility to children and adolescents with severe obesity and comorbidities after review by a multidisciplinary team [7].

Wikipedia reports studies in patients aged 5 to 21 showing weight loss comparable to adults, and a 2016 study found growth unaffected in children under 14 [1]. Before surgery, clinicians screen for psychiatric conditions, which Wikipedia's bariatric surgery article describes as common among candidates and important to assess [4].

Weight loss comes from smaller stomach volume and from removal of the portion that produces ghrelin, the hormone that stimulates appetite.[1] Wikipedia also notes improvements in glucose handling before major weight loss has occurred, which it relates to reduced gastric volume, changes in gut peptides and expression of genes involved in glucose absorption.[1]

Reviews note that the metabolic effects of bariatric surgery appear to exceed what weight loss alone would explain, and that changes to gastric emptying and gut hormones alter glucose handling [14][15].

A 2014 JAMA systematic review of long-term follow-up after bariatric surgery assessed weight loss and the course of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia in severely obese adults and noted the limited number of long-term studies with good retention.[3]

Wikipedia reports typical excess-weight loss of 50-70% over two years and cites a 2021 Lancet meta-analysis of 174,772 participants linking bariatric surgery to a 59% reduction in all-cause mortality in obese adults with type 2 diabetes and 30% without.[1] Studies in non-morbidly obese patients with diabetes have examined effects on insulin secretion.[16] A 2022 meta-analysis found better weight loss at 3 and 5 years after banded versus non-banded sleeve gastrectomy with no difference in comorbidity outcomes.[10]

Reviews note that the metabolic effects of bariatric surgery appear to exceed what weight loss alone would explain, and that changes to gastric emptying alter glucose handling.[14][15] Wikipedia also describes use in children and adolescents, endorsed by the International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders and the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, with weight loss comparable to adults.[1]

The SLEEVEPASS trial randomised 240 patients in Finland (121 to sleeve, 119 to bypass) between 2008 and 2010. At five years, mean excess-weight loss was 49 percent after sleeve and 57 percent after bypass, and the trial did not meet its equivalence criteria; diabetes remission was 37 and 45 percent and overall morbidity 19 and 26 percent, with no treatment-related deaths [6]. The ten-year report in JAMA Surgery found that both groups kept substantial weight loss, with bypass about 8.4 percentage points higher in excess-weight loss; remission of diabetes, dyslipidaemia and sleep apnoea did not differ significantly, hypertension remission was higher after bypass (24 versus 8 percent), and reoperation rates were similar (15.7 versus 18.5 percent) [6].

Weight loss after the operation reduces body fat and changes body shape, and patients describe visible changes in the face and body as weight comes off. Wikipedia's bariatric surgery article notes that excess skin can appear after major weight loss, that body-contouring surgery can address the arms, abdomen, thighs, buttocks and breasts, and that these changes unfold gradually over years [4].

Appearance research is small. A 2015 prospective study in Archives of Plastic Surgery photographed 14 patients (3 men, 11 women) before and 3 to 6 months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and had online lay raters estimate age and attractiveness. Mean weight loss was 20 percent of initial body weight; post-operative photos scored higher for attractiveness by a mean 0.256 points on a 10-point scale, six patients were judged significantly or non-significantly older, five younger and three unchanged, and the authors reported that mild weight loss tended to look younger but less attractive while larger loss looked older but more attractive, based largely on visual inspection of scatter plots [17]. The study was of bypass rather than sleeve patients, and the authors noted its short follow-up [17].

Wikipedia also reports that depression symptoms consistently fall after bariatric surgery and that some studies describe better body image and self-esteem [4]. Reviews of nutritional outcomes note that rapid weight loss can accompany micronutrient deficiencies that clinicians monitor after the sleeve [18].

Clinical guidance described by Wikipedia calls for lifelong multivitamin supplementation, soft protein-forward eating early on at roughly 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg a day, and avoiding alcohol for six months to a year; it notes that adherence to supplements is reported below 20 percent [4]. Deficiencies in iron, vitamin D, B12, folate, thiamine and fat-soluble vitamins are described as common [4]. One 2025 T Nation poster described losing 140 pounds in 2.5 years after a sleeve and keeping it off, while another described going from 25 stone to about 12 stone after a diet phase and then a sleeve, before turning to training [19][20].

In looksmaxxing and body-transformation communities the sleeve appears as the outer end of the weight-loss options, discussed beside diet, GLP-1 drugs and, in some threads, as part of a plan to lose weight before facial or body procedures. A 2013 Hacker News thread asked whether a sleeve could be used to 'hack' weight, reflecting that framing [21]. Forum users on T Nation discuss the sleeve alongside testosterone treatment, training and newer weight-loss peptides [19][20].

Cost and access shape where patients have it done, and some travel abroad for surgery. An October 2025 RNZ report said more New Zealanders were travelling overseas for surgery under medical tourism and that experts warn consequences can be severe [22].

A newer comparison is with GLP-1 medicines. A real-world study presented at the ASMBS 2025 annual meeting, published in Obesity, followed adults with a BMI of at least 35 and reported total weight loss at one, two and three years of about 24, 22 and 22 percent for sleeve gastrectomy, against roughly 5, 6.5 and 7 percent for semaglutide and 9 to 11 percent for tirzepatide; the society summarised surgery patients as losing about five times as much at two years [8]. The society that presented it represents bariatric surgeons, and the study was observational [8].

Large trials have compared the operation with others: a registered trial of sleeve gastrectomy versus gastric bypass enrolled 280 patients, one comparing gastric bypass, band and sleeve enrolled 1,351, and the BEST trial enrolled 1,752.[23][24][25] A trial in older patients compared sleeve and bypass.[26] Smaller randomized trials have examined analgesia after sleeve surgery, day-case discharge, omentopexy and gastric dilation, and anesthetic reversal.[27][28][29][30]

Observational work includes a review of gastric dilation after sleeve gastrectomy as a sole operation and a study of liraglutide for insufficient weight loss or regain after bariatric surgery.[12][31]

The SLEEVEPASS ten-year report found esophagitis in 31 percent of sleeve patients versus 7 percent after bypass, with more reflux symptoms and proton-pump inhibitor use, while de novo Barrett oesophagus was uncommon at 4 percent in each group [6].

A systematic analysis of 4,888 patients examined staple-line leak, described as an ongoing concern, and a World Journal of Gastroenterology review covers its prevention and management.[32][33] Wikipedia lists leak (about 1 in 200 patients), blood clots (about 1%), wound infection (about 10 to 15%), strictures (about 3.5%), reflux, nausea, vitamin B12 deficiency, reduced bone health, depression and weight regain among complications.[1]

A review of 118 cases described Wernicke encephalopathy after bariatric surgery, including after sleeve procedures, and advised testing and treating thiamine deficiency.[34] Case reports describe gastric twist obstruction after laparoscopic sleeve.[35] The operation is irreversible, and revision surgery or drugs such as liraglutide are used when weight loss is insufficient or weight is regained.[31][11]
The SLEEVEPASS authors concluded that pre-operative reflux assessment and patient selection matter, noting the higher esophagitis rate after sleeve [6].

lore.intro: The gastric sleeve appears in lifting and ascension forums mainly as a weight-loss route for people with severe obesity, often compared with injectable weight-loss drugs [19][21].

claims.claim: The sleeve produces far more weight loss than drugs or diet alone
Weight loss from surgery makes the face look better
The sleeve is a one-time fix
Surgery abroad is a cheap equivalent of surgery at home
The sleeve carries no lasting risks once healed

Sleeve becomes the most commonly performed bariatric operation.[4]
